Side A: HC diet in physically active adults; triglycerides increased from baseline 76 to 104 mg/dL after 3 weeks HC diet, p=0.005. Extraction looks correct: within-group change, direction '+', significant.

Side B: Pharm-TCR low-carb energy-restricted diet in type 2 diabetes; triglycerides improved (reduction), p<0.0001. Extraction seems faithful; comparison type marked unclear honestly.

Comparability: exposures differ — HC diet vs low-carb energy-restricted diet. Both diets, but opposite macronutrient composition. Outcomes: triglycerides. Contrast: A is within-group change from baseline under HC diet; B is improvement (reduction) with low-carb diet, contrast type unclear.

Are these comparable? Different diets (HC vs LC + energy restriction), different populations (healthy active adults vs T2D), different durations (3 weeks vs 12 weeks). The exposures are essentially opposite dietary interventions. The findings: HC diet increased triglycerides; LC diet decreased triglycerides. These are opposite directions for triglycerides with different diets.

Is this apparent_contradiction or contradictory or not_comparable? The exposures differ materially: HC diet vs LC energy-restricted diet. These are different interventions — comparing effect of HC diet on TG vs effect of LC diet on TG. Actually they could be seen as contrasting ends of carbohydrate intake; the abstracts themselves: A compares HC vs LC diets and found TG increased after HC. B tested LC diet vs TAU and found TG improved.

Hmm. Do the two findings "concern a sufficiently similar exposure"? Both are dietary carbohydrate manipulation with triglyceride outcome. One could argue they're comparable in a broad sense: high-carb raises TG, low-carb lowers TG — actually these are concordant in the physiological sense (carbohydrate intake positively associated with TG). Direction: A: HC → TG increase (+). B: LC diet → TG decrease (-). If we frame exposure as carbohydrate restriction vs high carbohydrate, the directions are consistent: more carbs → higher TG. But strictly, the exposures are different diets.

Analogously, HC diet and LC diet are different interventions, but they're on opposite ends of the same dietary spectrum. Comparing "HC diet increases TG" with "LC diet decreases TG" — these are opposite findings if we treat diet composition as the exposure axis. Actually they're not contradictory; they're complementary: high carb raises, low carb lowers — consistent with a dose-response.

But the decision framework: are the findings opposite? A says HC diet increased TG. B says LC energy-restricted diet decreased TG. If exposures were the same, opposite directions = contradiction. But exposures differ (HC vs LC + energy restriction). The framework says different population/dose may still permit contextual comparison. Here the exposure itself differs in a way that could explain the opposite direction — that's a text-supported contextual difference: A's intervention is high-carbohydrate/low-fat; B's is low-carbohydrate with energy restriction. Common factors in such schemas: population, intervention, outcome, comparison_type, duration, other, none, unknown. I'll pick "intervention" (exposure difference) — the diets differ (HC vs LC + energy restriction), and populations differ (healthy active adults vs T2D).

Alternatively, one could argue not_comparable because exposures differ. But the framework says "Different population, dose or method may still permit contextual comparison; do not exclude every difference mechanically." The findings are directly on the same outcome (triglycerides) with dietary carbohydrate level as the differing exposure — this is a classic apparent contradiction setup: opposite directions explained by differing intervention.

Opposite findings with a text-supported explanatory difference (different diets) → apparent_contradiction.

Yes, opposite at the abstract level, and the differing intervention (HC vs LC, plus energy restriction and population) explains it. That fits apparent_contradiction.

Alternatively not_comparable: different exposures (HC vs LC diets), different populations, different contrast types. But the guideline explicitly warns against mechanically excluding every difference. The outcome is identical (triglycerides), both dietary interventions differing in carbohydrate content — a meaningful comparison exists. I'll go apparent_contradiction.

verdict.label: apparent_contradiction
verdict.rationale: Both extractions are faithful to their sources. Side A reports that a three-week high-carbohydrate/low-fat diet significantly increased triglycerides within physically active adults (76 to 104 mg/dL; p = 0.005); side B reports clinically meaningful improvement (reduction) in triglycerides with a low-carbohydrate (<50 g), energy-restricted diet in people with type 2 diabetes (all p < 0.0001). The abstract-level directions for triglycerides are opposite. The sources themselves describe materially different interventions along the same dietary-carbohydrate axis: A tested a high-carbohydrate/low-fat diet for three weeks in healthy active adults, while B tested a low-carbohydrate, energy-restricted diet for 12 weeks in type 2 diabetes. This text-supported difference in exposure (plus population and duration) could explain the opposite triglyceride directions, so the pair is an apparent contradiction rather than a true one. A secondary limitation is that side B's contrast type (within-group change vs between-group vs TAU) is not specified in the abstract, but the extraction honestly flags this and it does not establish a material extraction error.

source_evidence.quote: Total cholesterol and LDL-cholesterol significantly decreased after the HC diet (97.9 ± 33.6 mg/dL at baseline to 78.2 ± 23.5 mg/dL; p = 0.02) while triglycerides significantly increased (76 ± 38 mg/dL at baseline to 104 ± 44 mg/dL; p = 0.005).

The present study investigated the impact of a three-week period of HC/low-fat (HC) diet followed by a three-week wash-out-phase and subsequent LC diet on the parameters of physical capacity assessed via cardiopulmonary exercise testing, body composition via bioimpedance analysis and blood profiles, which were assessed after each of the respective diet periods.
These reductions occurred concurrently with clinically meaningful improvements in hemoglobin A1C, anthropometrics, blood pressure, and triglycerides (all p < 0.0001).

We conducted a 12-week pragmatic, community-based parallel-group randomized controlled trial (ClinicalTrials.gov: NCT03181165) evaluating the effect of a low-carbohydrate (<50 g), energy-restricted diet (~850-1100 kcal/day; Pharm-TCR; n = 98) compared to treatment-as-usual (TAU; n = 90), delivered by community pharmacists, on glucose-lowering medication use, cardiometabolic health, and health-related quality of life.

diagnostics.notes: Side B's comparison.type is 'unclear' because the abstract does not specify whether the triglyceride improvement is a within-group change or a between-group difference versus TAU; this is a diagnostic limitation, not a material extraction error. Factor 'other' is used because the decisive supported contextual difference is the opposing dietary exposure itself (high-carbohydrate/low-fat vs low-carbohydrate energy-restricted), together with differing populations (physically active adults vs type 2 diabetes) and durations (3 vs 12 weeks).
